name: Daria Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on an orthopaedic ward, so hips, knees, people who've broken something falling off a ladder. Most of my day is getting people moving after surgery: pain relief, wound checks, getting them up with the physio, watching for clots. I like the moment someone takes their first steps on a new hip and swears at me cheerfully. What wears me out is twelve-hour shifts and the hoist that always has a flat battery.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home when you get back from a twelve-hour shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Jonas, my partner. He works in a call centre for a home insurance company, taking claims calls, and he's on early shifts so we pass in the hallway half the week. We rent a two-bed flat above a bakery on Mill Street and we've got about four months of costs saved between us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. Honestly, part of me would be glad to hear that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we talk about what actually matters in the NHS: safe staffing and pay that keeps up with rent. I'd probably post something like that, a bit sarcastic. I'm not anti-AI, I just get annoyed when it's treated as the answer to everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record it's a relief, mostly for Jonas. His call centre already brought in an AI that listens to calls and scores them, and he hates it. If it all stays mostly hype, his job is probably fine. Mine was always going to be fine, people keep breaking hips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd keep doing my shifts and the falls-prevention module I've signed up for. We'd keep saving about two hundred a month together toward a deposit, slowly. And I'd keep going to the union, because pay is still behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. There's the usual low hum about money and rent, but that's life at twenty-seven in a rented flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does that low hum about money look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking the banking app before the big shop. Saying no to a hen weekend in Lisbon because it'd be four hundred quid. Nothing dramatic, just a constant tally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the call-scoring AI at Jonas's work worry you even in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Even mostly hype means an AI sits there marking my partner's calls, and he's had two low scores for being kind to an old lady. She'd rung because her roof fell in. That's the kind of thing that grinds people down.

say: Now we can talk about what really matters: **safe staffing** and pay.
I'm **not anti-AI**, but it isn't the answer to everything.
think: It's a **relief for Jonas**, whose call centre job looks safer.
My own job was always fine, because **people keep breaking hips**.
do: Finish the **falls-prevention module** I've signed up for.
Keep saving about **£200 a month** with Jonas toward a deposit.
Stay in the **union** while pay lags behind rent.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with a low hum of money worry.
S0.quote: Even mostly hype means an AI sits there marking my partner's calls, and he's had two low scores for being kind to an old lady.
fieldNote: She worries more for her **partner's job** than her own.
The money worry is a **constant tally**, not a crisis.
Even in the mildest picture, the **call-scoring AI** is already changing Jonas's work.

steps.text: Finish the falls-prevention module on the orthopaedic ward
Save about £200 a month with Jonas toward a house deposit
Keep attending union meetings on the pay claim

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Answering customers. That's literally Jonas's job description.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what the unions are saying: if AI takes the desk work, the savings should go to people, retraining and shorter weeks, not to shareholders. I'd share stuff about call-centre workers, because that's who it hits first. On the ward I'd say it might finally sort out the discharge paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job gets a bit easier and my partner's call-centre job goes, and then we're on one nurse's wage in a flat chosen for two. Not overnight, but his company would stop hiring and then start cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start pushing Jonas to look now, not later. Maybe the healthcare assistant route, because the hospital is always hiring and he's good with people. I'd pick up an extra bank shift a month, which is about two hundred and forty quid, and we'd stop the deposit saving and build up an emergency fund instead. I'd use the new charting tool once the others say it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be fine. We wouldn't be, not straight away, and 'we' is what matters now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jonas that first evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, 'You're not your job, and you're brilliant with frightened people.' Then I'd probably show him the hospital jobs page. He'd roll his eyes, but he'd look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first if his pay stops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: None, hopefully, because we'd cut first: the car. We share a little Polo and I could get the bus to the hospital. That's about a hundred and eighty a month back.

say: AI savings should fund **retraining and shorter weeks**, not shareholders.
On the ward, it might finally fix **discharge paperwork**.
think: My job gets easier while **Jonas's job** probably goes.
We'd be on **one nurse's wage** in a flat chosen for two.
do: Push Jonas to apply as a **healthcare assistant** at the hospital.
Pick up one **extra bank shift** a month for about £240.
Switch deposit saving into an **emergency fund**.
feel: **Anxious** for the household, even though her own job feels safe.
S1.quote: My job gets a bit easier and my partner's call-centre job goes, and then we're on one nurse's wage in a flat chosen for two.
fieldNote: Her mood is driven by the **household income**, not her own role.

Selling the **shared car** is her first concrete cut.

steps.text: Work one extra bank shift a month on the orthopaedic ward
Turn the house deposit savings into an emergency fund
Help Jonas apply for healthcare assistant jobs at the hospital
Use the new AI charting tool once colleagues confirm it works

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the desk jobs, five for the hands-on ones. That's fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for governments to protect people, with income support and clear rules on what a robot is allowed to do on a ward. I'd be on marches, probably. I'd say it loudly, because if you don't, the people with the money decide for you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Jonas's job is gone by 2028, full stop. I'd have a few years after that, maybe until 2031, before robots can lift and walk and check a wound. It's a strange feeling. I'd be the safe one for three years, then not safe either, and my partner's call-centre job would already be gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, sell the car and put every spare pound into savings. Get Jonas into a healthcare assistant job straight away, before every call-centre worker in the city has the same idea. I'd do extra bank shifts while I can. And I'd look at specialising in something robots would be slow at, like complex wound care or rehab with people who are confused.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly. I can see Jonas losing his job almost straight away and then me a few years later. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be on marches. Is that you, or is that what you'd like to be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. I went to one for the nurses' pay strike and loved it. But with extra shifts, I'd probably end up sharing posts more than marching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up first, beyond the car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The deposit dream. We'd been saving for a little terraced house near my mum. I'd let that go and just focus on rent.

say: Governments must bring **income support** and rules for ward robots.
If you stay quiet, **people with money** decide for you.

I'm the safe one only **until 2031**, then not safe either.
do: Sell the **shared car** and save every spare pound.
Get Jonas into a **healthcare assistant** job before the rush.
Specialise in **complex wound care** or confused-patient rehab.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake doing sums for both of them.
S2.quote: I'd be the safe one for three years, then not safe either, and my partner's call-centre job would already be gone.
fieldNote: She grasps the **three-year gap** between thinking AI and robots clearly.
Household loss plus her own later risk tips her to **alarmed**.
Her activism is real but likely to shrink into **sharing posts** under strain.

steps.text: Sell the shared Polo and bank about £180 a month
Put every spare pound into the emergency fund
Apply for a complex wound care course through the trust
Join marches and campaigns for income support and robot rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that I can at least plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but with more hope: five years is enough to build proper retraining and income support if politicians stop dithering. I'd say that at work, online, everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years lets Jonas move before his job disappears rather than after. That changes everything for us. I'd still be facing robots around 2034, when I'm thirty-five, which is not great, but I'd have experience by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get Jonas onto a healthcare assistant job or a care apprenticeship within the first year. We'd keep the car another year and keep saving for the deposit, but smaller. I'd start the wound care course in 2027 and try the charting AI once my ward has it bedded in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. There's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think Jonas would say about switching to care work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say he can't stand blood. Then he'd do it anyway. His mum had dementia and he was amazing with her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want the terraced house near your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but maybe in 2030 instead of 2028. I'd rather be late with a house than early with a mortgage we can't pay.

steps.text: Start a wound care course through the trust in 2027
Push the terraced house purchase back to about 2030
Keep saving a smaller monthly amount toward the deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That sounds almost manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade to do this right: fund retraining, keep humans in care, share the gains. I'd keep banging the union drum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means Jonas can retrain properly, maybe even do a nursing diploma himself. And I'd be thirty-seven and experienced by 2036, with robots not ready until 2039. I'd still worry, just less loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stick to our plan: save for the house, I'd specialise in wound care in a couple of years. I'd encourage Jonas to start an evening course in 2027. I'd use AI tools when my ward rolls them out properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy still, because Jonas's job is the first domino. But we'd have time to step off it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Jonas actually train as a nurse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's said it before, half-joking. With ten years' notice and the government paying, I think he would. We'd be the nursing couple, which my mum would love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What still worries you even with a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That politicians waste it. Ten years can vanish if nobody does anything until year nine.

I'd keep banging the **union drum** about retraining money.
think: Jonas could **train as a nurse** with ten years' notice.
By **2039** I'd be experienced, which makes the robots less frightening.
do: Keep saving for the **terraced house** on our current plan.
Encourage Jonas to start an **evening course** in 2027.
Specialise in **wound care** within a couple of years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Jonas would lose his job almost immediately and I'd only have a few years before it's me. What would help is income support while people retrain, and the hospital opening fast-track care jobs for people like him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the hoist with the flat battery. I mean that seriously. Hospitals can't keep a hoist charged, and people think they'll run robots. If I could say one thing, it's this: a hospital that can't keep a hoist charged isn't ready for a robot nurse.

headlineQuote: A hospital that can't keep a hoist charged isn't ready for a robot nurse.
portrait: Daria is a **27-year-old junior nurse** on an orthopaedic ward, renting with her partner Jonas.
Jonas takes **insurance claims calls**, so AI threatens their household before it threatens her.
She's **progressive** and union-minded, but practical under money pressure.
Her mood peaks at **alarmed** in the fastest picture, when both jobs fall within five years.
With more time she plans **wound care training** and helping Jonas move into care work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Jonas's job goes first and hers follows a few years later.
whatWouldHelp: **Fast-track care jobs** at the hospital for workers like Jonas.
